summary.text:
Hounslow's 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy Statement, approved at Borough Council on 3 March 2026 (already heard at Audit and Governance on 3 February and Cabinet on 10 February). A 43-page standalone strategy with ten annexes carrying every figure inside — CFR, prudential indicators, MRP policy, liability benchmark chart and MUFG interest rate forecast are all in this file. No officer email addresses published in the appendix. The statutory S151 is the Executive Director of Finance and Resources (title verified from paras 9.5 and Annex H); paper does not name them.

The distinctive story is externalisation. Under-borrowing shrinks from £197.3m actual at 31 March 2025 to £111.2m estimated at 31 March 2029 — £86.1m of internal borrowing closed across four years. Paras 15.1 and 15.2 frame this deliberately: 'From April 2023, it was clear that this would no longer be possible' to fund the CFR from internal resources, so external borrowing rises from £608.1m in April 2025 to a forecast £931.3m by March 2029, with £30m of that being explicit externalisation of internal HRA borrowing. Runs opposite to Camden, Cheshire West, Milton Keynes and others widening internal borrowing in the same window. Balance-sheet identity ties at every year of the plan.

Two MRP policy changes for 2026/27, both lengthening asset lives and reducing the annual charge — pre-2007/08 supported borrowing moves from 4% reducing balance to 50-year straight-line (Option 3), and post-2007/08 unsupported asset lives extend from about 15 years to a maximum of 50 years. A third change moves loans-to-third-parties MRP (£228.3m CFR) to Option 3 annuity basis to match rental streams. The annuity discount rate is set as the PWLB new loan annuity rate at 1 April of the year MRP commences, relevant to the asset life period — the same construction as Tower Hamlets. Paper explicitly notes this is the first year the discount rate has been disclosed.

Loan-book reconciliation does NOT tie exactly. Our file today carries 27 live PWLB loans at £591.5m and 3.858% weighted; their 31 December 2025 print is £521.5m at 3.85% (rate ties to two decimal places; principal difference consistent with January-August 2026 drawings out of the £94m planned Jan-Mar 2026 lift). Cannot claim a clean tie so the loan-book claim is kept out of the email lead. Break-cost position (indicative, DMO curve at 14/8/26) is a net £98.7m discount on the priced £590.2m, dominated by four loans of 2.44-3.16% maturing 2072/2073, but is not quoted in the email in an unbounded way given the reconciliation caveat.

Other notable items: £34.5m of LOBOs plus £7.5m market loans (no option), all 2006-2010 vintage; a £10m LOBO option window passed in February 2026 with outcome not disclosed in the paper; £226.3m of Council lending to Lampton Investment 360 Ltd with a proposed deed of variation to allow interest capitalisation on the balance (S151 seeking delegated authority to sign); and a first-ever CMI issuance of £1m at 4.10% in June-September 2025 — Hounslow is only the fourth council we have read that carries any CMI. HRA financing cost ratio moves 22.2% → 19.4% → 20.2% → 21.2% → 19.9% — rising through the middle years as HRA borrowing lifts £86m and £30m of internal borrowing is externalised.

Email drafted around three findings: the externalisation trajectory (£86m closed over four years, against the peer direction), the MRP annuity discount rate (a rate we publish daily, and their first year disclosing the choice), and the CMI first issuance (uncommon financing tool). Rate cross-check disclosed as scoped ('today vs your 31 December'), not framed as a full reconciliation. Meeting has passed so the send-by targets the autumn mid-year update. Draft not sendable until an officer email is confirmed; addressed at Executive Director of Finance and Resources level per the statutory S151 delegation in Annex H.

officer.subject: £86m of internal borrowing closed across four years — the opposite direction to most
officer.body:
Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy ahead of the autumn mid-year update to Audit and Governance. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your strategy is one of the more disclosive ones we've read this year, which is why several of the observations below could only be made because you actually wrote them down.

As a light cross-check before anything else: the weighted average rate on our current PWLB file for you sits at 3.858%, against your 3.85% in Table 2 at 31 December. Principal is different because our snapshot is today and yours is year-end, with new drawings in between, so we don't claim a full loan-book tie — just noting the rate agrees.

The distinctive thing in the strategy is the direction of travel on internal borrowing. Your Table 4 has under-borrowing shrinking from £197.3m at March 2025 to £111.2m by March 2029 — £86m closed across four years, driven partly by the £30m HRA externalisation you flag explicitly. That runs opposite to most of the strategies we've read this year, where the direction is the other way — internal borrowing widening because market rates make holding cash more attractive than borrowing it. Your paragraphs 15.1 and 15.2 give a clear reason for the opposite call (April 2023 as the point at which internal resources could no longer carry the CFR). It's worth flagging because most reports would have buried the explanation and yours doesn't.

The MRP piece worth noting is quiet but recurring in our reading. Your annuity discount rate for Option 3 is set as the PWLB new loan annuity rate at 1 April of the year MRP commences, relevant to the asset life. That's the same construction Tower Hamlets uses and — because it's a rate we publish daily on pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis alongside every other PWLB tenor — the discount rate you'll apply on 1 April 2027 is something you can look up on the day rather than commission. Your Annex C also states this is the first year you've disclosed the choice of discount rate, which most councils quietly leave undisclosed. Worth reading alongside the £228m loans-to-third-parties CFR that this policy sits under.

And the CMI: your first issuance between June and September 2025 (£1m at 4.10%, Table 2) makes Hounslow only the fourth council carrying any CMI in the papers we've read. Camden holds £1m at 1.75%; Hammersmith & Fulham holds £3.5m across five Green Investment tranches. It is a small line in your table and a niche instrument sector-wide, but if the pipeline behind it is real then the peer set for how councils have run subsequent tranches is short and every one is documented.

For a sense of where the curve has moved since your MUFG forecast (22 December 2025): the December view had Mar 2026 Bank at 3.75% (correct on the day), 25-year certainty at 5.80% and 50-year at 5.60%. Our daily PWLB certainty publication is where you can test the rest of the December path against what actually happened. Monthly sector picture is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, three look relevant to Hounslow specifically. Cost of carry and internal borrowing, for the £154.9m of under-borrowing at your March 2026 estimate and the £30m HRA externalisation planned for 2026/27. MRP options and Regulation 27, given the two policy changes for 2026/27 and the £228m loans-to-third-parties stream. And our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members there's an Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) course, written for exactly the committee your mid-year update will next go to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
